concept.name: Herding
concept.definition: The tendency of individuals to suppress their own judgment and conform to the behavior of the group; in financial markets, the clustering of investors into the same trades, driven by conformity, information cascades, and reputational concerns. It is a documented behavioral pattern associated with bubbles, panics, and momentum, not a reliable signal in itself.
concept.intuition: When everyone is buying, not buying feels wrong; the crowd feels like information even when it is just a crowd.
concept.mechanics: Conformity experiments (Asch) show roughly a third of subjects following an obviously wrong majority; in markets, Keynes's 'better to fail conventionally' logic, information cascades, and social proof produce correlated buying and selling that amplifies trends and crashes. The SEC-commissioned Library of Congress report lists following the herd among the systematic mistakes of U.S. investors.
concept.failure_modes: Herding can be individually rational (career risk, genuine information in others' actions), so correlated trades are not automatically irrational. Contrarian strategies built against herding can lose for long stretches while the crowd is right.
concept.misconceptions: Herding is not simply copying smart money - cascades form even when most participants privately doubt the consensus. Nor is every correlated market move herding; common reactions to public news are a different phenomenon.
concept.example: During a meme-stock spike, retail traders buy because everyone else is buying and posting gains, pushing the price far beyond any fundamental anchor until the cascade reverses.

citations.source: Behavioral Patterns and Pitfalls of U.S. Investors (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, prepared for the U.S. SEC, August 2010)
citations.section: Overview, p. 1; Manias and Panics section, p. 11
